title: Capelli’s theorem and polynomial composition
subject: criteria
summary: Capelli’s theorem reduces irreducibility of a composition to irreducibility over a root field. Power classes and norms then give criteria for binomials and iterates.
field: general fields; characteristic zero for binomials
questionsAnswered: When is a composition of polynomials irreducible?
Exactly when is a binomial irreducible in characteristic zero?
How can one prove irreducibility of every iterate?

sections.title: Capelli’s composition theorem
sections.body:
Theorem · Capelli's composition lemma

Let \(K\) be any field, let \(F\in K[x]\) be irreducible of degree \(m\ge1\), and let \(g\in K[x]\) have degree \(d\ge1\). For a root \(\alpha\) of \(F\), the composition \(F(g(x))\) is irreducible over \(K\) if and only if \(g(x)-\alpha\) is irreducible over \(K(\alpha)\).

Proof

Choose a root \(\beta\) of \(g(x)-\alpha\). Since \(\alpha=g(\beta)\), we have \(K(\alpha)\subseteq K(\beta)\), and

\[[K(\beta):K]=m\,[K(\beta):K(\alpha)].\]

The polynomial \(F(g(x))\), of degree \(md\), has root \(\beta\). It is irreducible exactly when the left side is \(md\), equivalently when the minimal polynomial of \(\beta\) over \(K(\alpha)\) has degree \(d\). No separability assumption is needed for this argument.

The composition problem is thus reduced to irreducibility over a root field. When \(g=x^r+c\), the new question is whether \(x^r-(\alpha-c)\) factors; power classes and norms give useful criteria.

citations.note: Capelli’s composition lemma, stated for arbitrary fields.
Composition and reducibility in extension fields.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

Both \(F=x^2-8\) and \(g=x^2-3\) are irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), but

\[F(g(x))=x^4-6x^2+1=(x^2-2x-1)(x^2+2x-1).\]

For \(\alpha=2\sqrt2\), we have \(3+\alpha=(1+\sqrt2)^2\), so \(g(x)-\alpha\) splits in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)[x]\). Irreducibility of the two inputs over \(\mathbb Q\) does not exclude this square in the root field.

citations.note: The root-field criterion explains the explicitly verified example.

sections.title: Capelli’s binomial criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · Capelli's binomial criterion

Let \(K\) have characteristic zero, \(a\in K^\times\), and \(n\ge2\). Then \(x^n-a\) is irreducible over \(K\) exactly when

  • \(a\notin K^p\) for every prime \(p\mid n\);
  • if \(4\mid n\), then \(a\notin-4K^4\).

Here \(K^p=\{b^p:b\in K\}\). This statement is restricted to characteristic zero; finite-field questions are treated separately.

The first obstruction gives a difference-of-powers factorization. The exceptional fourth-power obstruction comes from

\[x^{4r}+4b^4=(x^{2r}-2bx^r+2b^2)(x^{2r}+2bx^r+2b^2).\]

These prove necessity. The proof of sufficiency uses successive prime-power extensions and excludes powers in the intermediate root fields. Odd-prime steps use norms; the power of two requires precisely the additional obstruction above.

Example

The polynomial \(x^4+4\) factors by the displayed identity even though \(-4\) is not a rational square. In contrast, \(x^6-72\) is irreducible: \(72=2^3 3^2\) is neither a square nor a cube. In fact \(x^n-72\) is irreducible for every \(n\ge2\), because no prime divides both valuation exponents \(3,2\), and a positive rational number cannot be \(-4\) times a rational fourth power.

citations.note: The classical binomial reducibility theorem, including the exceptional fourth-power case.
The field-theoretic treatment of irreducible binomials and the norm argument.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

For \(h=x^6-72\), the Newton polygon at \(2\) has one slope \(-3/6=-1/2\), allowing proper factor degrees \(2,4\). At \(3\), its slope is \(-2/6=-1/3\), allowing only degree \(3\). The empty intersection gives a second proof of irreducibility, complementing Capelli. Neither polygon individually forces the full degree.

Let the positive root be \(\alpha=\sqrt2\sqrt[3]{3}\). The identities

\[\sqrt2=\alpha^3/6,\qquad\sqrt[3]{3}=\alpha^4/12\]

show that the splitting field is \(L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt[3]{3},\zeta_3)\). The splitting field \(M\) of \(x^3-3\) has group \(S_3\): the cubic is Eisenstein at \(3\), and its discriminant is \(-243\). Its unique quadratic subfield is \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})\). Thus \(M\cap\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)=\mathbb Q\), and restriction gives

\[\operatorname{Gal}(h/\mathbb Q)\cong S_3\times C_2,\qquad |\operatorname{Gal}(h/\mathbb Q)|=12.\]

The discriminant \(2^{21}3^{16}\) is nonsquare, but the group is much smaller than \(S_6\). The group calculation requires information beyond either irreducibility proof or the discriminant square class.

citations.note: The slope-denominator principle applied to the explicitly computed two-prime certificate.
Galois correspondence, composita, and the quadratic subfield determined by a discriminant; the displayed sextic calculation is supplied here.
The complementary binomial criterion.

sections.title: Irreducibility of quadratic iterates
sections.body:
Example · every iterate of \(f=x^2+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\)

Put \(F_r=f^{\circ r}\) and \(a_r=F_r(0)\), with \(a_0=0\). Then \(a_{r+1}=a_r^2+1\), beginning \(0,1,2,5,26,677\). The base case \(F_1=x^2+1\) is irreducible. Suppose \(F_r\) is irreducible and let \(\alpha\) be a root. Capelli reduces the next step to showing that \(\alpha-1\) is not a square in \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\).

Since \(F_r\) is monic of even degree,

\[N_{\mathbb Q(\alpha)/\mathbb Q}(\alpha-1)=F_r(1)=a_{r+1}=a_r^2+1.\]

For \(r\ge1\), this integer lies strictly between \(a_r^2\) and \((a_r+1)^2\). It is therefore not a rational square. A square in \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\) would have square norm, giving the contradiction and completing induction.

Remark

A nonsquare norm certifies a nonsquare element; a square norm does not certify a square element. The argument proves stability, meaning irreducibility of every iterate. Determining every Galois group in the resulting tree requires further information. The correction to Ayad–McQuillan withdraws a claimed converse in a broader stability criterion.

citations.note: Capelli’s lemma underlying the supplied norm induction.
The corrected sufficient stability criterion and the failure of the original converse.
Stability and its relation to arboreal Galois representations.

related.why: The tower formula turns polynomial irreducibility into an equality of extension degrees.
Stability gives transitivity at every level of an arboreal action.
The sextic x⁶−72 has both a Capelli proof and a proof using Newton polygons at two primes.
The sextic example has nonsquare discriminant and a Galois group of order 12.

questions.title: Does composition preserve irreducibility?
questions.body: No. The pair \(x^2-8\), \(x^2-3\) above is a counterexample. Capelli identifies the missing condition: the inner polynomial minus a root of the outer one must remain irreducible over that root field.

citations.note: The exact criterion, applied here to an independently expanded example.

title: Irreducibility from integer values
subject: criteria
summary: Unit, small, and prime values restrict the possible integral factors of a polynomial. Schur’s and Pólya’s criteria provide explicit examples.
questionsAnswered: Why is a product of distinct linear integer factors minus one irreducible?
How small must many values be to force irreducibility?
How many prime or unit values suffice?

sections.title: Schur’s unit-value problem
sections.body:
Theorem · the minus-one case of Schur's problem

For distinct integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\), with \(m\ge1\), the polynomial

\[P(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(x-a_i)-1\]

is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof

A nontrivial factorization gives monic \(g,h\in\mathbb Z[x]\) of positive degrees with \(P=gh\). At each \(a_i\), the integers \(g(a_i),h(a_i)\) multiply to \(-1\), so \(g(a_i)+h(a_i)=0\). The polynomial \(g+h\) has degree less than \(m\) and at least \(m\) distinct roots. It must vanish identically, contradicting the monicity of both factors.

For the plus-one polynomial, two exceptions are

\[x(x-2)+1=(x-1)^2,\qquad x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)+1=(x^2-3x+1)^2.\]

Westlund and Flügel's classical solution, recalled in Győry–Hajdu–Tijdeman, shows that these are the only reducible plus-one cases, up to an integer translation of the variable. Schur posed the question in 1908.

citations.note: The original problem, rather than an attribution of the later solution.
The minus-one theorem, the complete plus-one exception list, and attribution of the 1909 solution.

sections.title: Pólya’s criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · Pólya's criterion

Let \(P\in\mathbb Z[x]\) have degree \(n\ge2\), and put \(N=\lceil n/2\rceil\). If there are \(n\) distinct integers \(a\) such that

\[0\lt |P(a)|\lt \frac{N!}{2^N},\]

then \(P\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof

If \(P=QR\) with positive-degree integral factors, choose the larger degree \(d=\deg Q\), so \(N\le d\le n-1\). At every selected integer, \(|Q(a)|\le|P(a)|\), because the other integral factor is nonzero. Choose \(d+1\) of those arguments and order them as \(b_0\lt \cdots\lt b_d\). Their integer spacing gives \(\prod_{i\ne j}|b_j-b_i|\ge j!(d-j)!\). Writing \(M=\max_j|Q(b_j)|\), Lagrange interpolation gives

\[1\le|\operatorname{lc}(Q)|\le M\sum_{j=0}^{d}\frac1{j!(d-j)!}=M\frac{2^d}{d!}.\]

Consequently \(M\ge d!/2^d\ge N!/2^N\), contradicting the strict bound. Gauss's lemma justifies the integral factorization even when \(P\) is not monic.

Example

For \(P(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{9}(x-j)+2\), the ten values at \(0,\ldots,9\) are all \(2\). Since \(2\lt 5!/2^5=15/4\), Pólya proves irreducibility without expanding the polynomial. Nonzero values are essential: an integer zero would itself give a rational linear factor.

citations.note: The classical small-value irreducibility criterion.
Confirms the ceiling in N and the strict factorial threshold; the displayed interpolation proof is supplied here.

sections.title: A prime-value criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · prime and unit values

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be primitive of degree \(n\ge1\). If \(|f(a)|\) is either \(1\) or a prime at \(2n+1\) distinct integers \(a\), then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof

For a positive-degree integral factorization \(f=gh\), every selected argument satisfies \(g(a)=1\), \(g(a)=-1\), \(h(a)=1\), or \(h(a)=-1\). Those four equations have at most \(2\deg g+2\deg h=2n\) distinct solutions in total, a contradiction.

Example

At \(a=0,1,2,3,4\), the values of \(x^2+x+41\) are \(41,43,47,53,61\), all prime. Thus the criterion proves irreducibility. It says nothing about primality at all later arguments; at \(40\) the value is \(41^2\).

citations.note: The finite prime-or-unit-value criterion and its elementary counting proof.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.body:
Remark

A single prime value is insufficient: \((x-1)(x+1)\) takes the prime value \(3\) at \(2\). Conversely, \(x^2+x+4\) is irreducible because its discriminant is \(-15\), yet every integer value is even and at least \(4\). The preceding criterion does not apply.

A single prime value can suffice when extra information controls the factors: Cohn's criterion restricts the coefficients to base digits, while root bounds force nonconstant factors to have large absolute values at a chosen integer. For more general small-value criteria, Levit, Tverberg, and Győry–Hajdu–Tijdeman develop sharper bounds and extensions. The number and sizes of the values are essential hypotheses in these results.

questions.title: Must an irreducible integer polynomial take a prime or unit value?
questions.scope: Primitive polynomials in Z[x], with integer arguments and without changing variables
questions.body: No. The primitive irreducible polynomial \(x^2+x+4\) has only positive even values at integers, all at least \(4\). Thus the prime-value criterion is not necessary for irreducibility.

citations.note: The same explicit obstruction is recorded after the prime-value criterion. Proof in expository notes; this status records the unpublished source.
